newsitem.title: USA: US share of new NATO set at $200 mln a year - report.
newsitem.headline: US share of new NATO set at $200 mln a year - report.

text.p: Expansion of NATO will cost more than $30 billion over the next 12 years, but the U.S. share should be no more than $200 million a year, the Washington Post reported on Sunday.
The newspaper said the cost projections were contained in a 31-page European security strategy report that the Clinton administration would present to Congress on Monday.
The 16-nation NATO alliance will convene in July in Madrid to select the first group of new members from among 11 former communist countries of central and eastern Europe that are seeking to join.

The Post said it had obtained a near-final draft of the report which stressed that the cost projections were variable, depending on which countries joined, how the costs were allocated and what new missions NATO might decide to take on during the 12-year expansion.

To upgrade the armed forces of new members, integrate them into the NATO command structure and make them part of NATO's collective air defence system would cost $2.1 billion to $2.7 billion a year, according to the administration's estimates.

The Post quoted the report as saying that whatever the final figures, "these costs are affordable" and that the potential price of failing to expand NATO were greater than those of moving the alliance forward.

The newspaper said the report assumed that the new members selected at the Madrid summit would pick up 35 percent of the cost of joining, current members other than the United States would pay about 50 percent, and the United States would pay 15 percent.

That meant Washington's bill would be $150 million to $200 million a year, up to a maximum of about $2.5 billion, an amount the report described as a drop in the bucket in the overall $263 billion U.S. defence budget, the Post said.
